summary: A two-month running thread about one friendship: first a post-mortem on a 5 May exchange where Shereen opened up and he joked, withdrew, then explained himself; then his unilateral ending of the friendship on 13 June after a bad birthday; then her refusal of that ending, and the friendship turning romantic four days later. He asked repeatedly for diagnosis rather than drafted replies, and explicitly asked for pushback rather than agreement. What came out of it is a record of a decision he made and had overturned, one conversational method of his own, and several checkable claims about how he handles emotional pressure.

findings.title: Ending the friendship with Shereen, and reversing it four days later
findings.body:
On the morning of Friday 13 June 2025 he ended a platonic friendship with Shereen. The chain leading there: some weeks earlier she had told him, in a conversation outside her gate, that the friendship was becoming difficult because her feelings were stronger than his — he had been clear from the start that he only wanted friendship. He decided the responsible response was to carry on as normal while being careful not to lead her on. In the week before her birthday his own feelings shifted, and his behaviour changed with them: a perfunctory birthday message, a check-in, and a stray 'hb' posted in a group chat. She called it out directly — 'you were a bad friend on my birthday'.

His reasoning for ending it was not the change in feeling but the change in behaviour. He judged that the behaviour was the leading edge of a pattern he could not control, that his involvement was hurting them both, and that it put each of them in a poor position to meet a future spouse. Two of his stated principles are worth keeping. First, on why he chose severe pain over ambiguity: a decisive hurt 'is a hurt that will heal with time, whereas the uncertainty is a constant low-lying heartache that never really goes away.' Second, on why he made the call alone: 'It's never really been an option for me to do that, and whenever I did, it backfired in my face time after time.'

That same evening he stopped at her house to say goodbye and explained the full reasoning face to face. She pushed back and refused the ending outright, arguing that with all the context now on the table the situation was not unsalvageable. He accepted. By Monday 16 June they were holding hands at a viewpoint over the city, and she left the next day on a two-week trip home, which both treated as deliberate time apart to pray and evaluate before deciding how to proceed.

The decision was wrong, and it was wrong in precisely the way she had named — not in its content but in its being made alone.

findings.title: Stating your own assumptions out loud rather than questioning the other person's
findings.body:
His own proposal for the next stage with Shereen: schedule an open conversation where each person states their own assumptions aloud. The premise is specific — because their core values line up closely, the risk is not open disagreement but silent, unexamined assumptions about what the other believes or expects. Two outcomes are acceptable: either both parties are at peace that they are on the same page, or a mismatch surfaces that neither knew was there and can be discussed on the spot.

The distinguishing feature is direction. You state what you assume, not what you want to know about them. That puts the burden of exposure on the speaker and stops the conversation becoming an interrogation.

A workable structure for it: reflect and write privately first, then take turns completing sentence stems in three groups. About the other person — 'I assume you believe…', 'I assume you want…', 'I assume you would struggle with…'. About the relationship — 'I assume this is moving toward…', 'I assume we handle conflict by…', 'I assume our physical boundaries are…', 'I assume the timing of next steps looks like…'. About faith — how each sees Scripture, and who each is accountable to. Each statement gets one of three responses: agreement, 'my view is actually…', or 'I'm still working that out, can I come back to you after praying about it.' The aim is truthful overlap rather than complete overlap. Boundaries — emotional, physical and spiritual — belong inside the same conversation, and for both of them the Bible is the first source of truth on all three.

findings.title: The three-move failure sequence in the 5 May exchange
findings.body:
Worth keeping because the moves are his own sentences, not general advice, and the same sequence is what to watch for.

Move one — humour at a vulnerable opening. She wrote 'I feel fine but at the same time I feel very much not fine like I could cry because something inside feels wrong but I can't put my finger on what the wrong thing is.' He replied 'Sounds like a Monday 🙃'. She answered 'Did I mention a day or my emotional state?' It was not intended as a joke, but the levity read as detachment.

Move two — taking a guarded answer at face value. After he asked 'Tell me what's going through your mind bruv' she said 'It's fine don't worry about me… God is carrying it with me.' He stepped back: 'You also said it's between you and God, so that's fine. I don't need to get in the middle of that.' Her response was that this was not a boundary he was honouring, it was self-protection he had accepted as dismissal — 'now that I'm giving you what you clearly want which is distance from my emotions'.

Move three — explaining his own confusion. 'I'm not sure how to proceed further conversationally in a way that would actually help you… I'm just doing something instead of being silent… I don't know.' Sincere, but it made his uncertainty the subject and left her to manage it.

Then a full day of silence while he worked out what to say — which, to someone who had just written that she feels disposable, is the shape of the thing she was afraid of. His stated intent was to understand before responding rather than make it worse. The corrective is not to reply instantly but to name the pause: say that you are taking time to respond well, so the gap is legible as care rather than withdrawal.

findings.title: Treats his own behaviour, not his feelings, as the reliable signal
findings.body:
He distrusts his emotions as evidence and reads his actions instead: 'I strongly distrust my emotions (and for good reasons) but before I've even had time to scrutinize how I feel and validate if my emotions are real or just circumstantial, my actions have already told me everything that I needed to know.' In practice this means he acts on a behavioural change in himself before he has finished interrogating the feeling behind it — the behaviour is treated as the diagnosis.

The specific pattern he watches for was named for him by a friend, who told him it was textbook and had been true for as long as they had known him: when someone close begins to pull away, he does not withdraw in return; some time later he pulls toward them. He calls it panicked detachment, describes it as trauma-bond-like, says it is one of the emotional responses he has never been able to control, and says the road it leads down has previously devastated more than one person who cared for him.
findings.counter_evidence: The trigger condition did not actually hold this time. Shereen said plainly 'I wasn't pulling away from you at all', and by his own account she was right — she had been trying to respect the limit he set. What he did on her birthday was withdraw, not pull toward her, which is the opposite of the pattern he was invoking. He also adopted the label within days on one friend's off-the-cuff assessment and ended a friendship over it, which sits badly with the claim that he scrutinises before acting. And when Shereen pushed back in person that evening he reversed within hours, so the reading is not as immovable as he presents it.

findings.title: Makes emotional decisions alone, and says he has never had the option not to
findings.body:
Asked why he had not let Shereen have a say in ending the friendship, he did not defend it as correct — he described it as the only mode available to him: 'It's never really been an option for me to do that, and whenever I did, it backfired in my face time after time. I definitely lack trust in that particular space.' She had identified the same thing as the sharpest part of the injury: 'now you've made a final decision without letting me be part of it. And honestly, that hurts even more than all the uncertainty did… I just wish you had trusted me enough to go through the messy, human part of this together.'

Note that the withholding is framed as protection. He believed ending it unilaterally was the responsible thing, and specifically that it would spare her worse harm later. The effect was to deny her the choice of accepting the risk with full information.
findings.counter_evidence: He conceded the point the same day it was made — 'I really could (should) have let you be a part of the final decision, I see that now' — and then actually reversed the decision that evening when she argued against it, which is the opposite of the pattern holding firm. It is also narrow rather than general: nothing here suggests he avoids decisions or avoids acting; the reluctance is specific to letting another person into a decision about the emotional relationship itself.

findings.title: Wants the diagnosis and refuses the script
findings.body:
Offered a drafted reply three separate times, he declined each time, and said why on the first: 'I don't want to become reliant on AI or external help to try and respond in the most correct way or whatever, just wanted to get out of my own head with this because it's causing me a mental block.' What he asked for instead was consistently analytical — what he got wrong in his own responses, a summary with steps to improve, and a cheat-sheet he could glance at the next time he felt the same block. He also controlled the sequencing deliberately, cutting off an offered framework mid-thread with 'Let's not get to the final part just yet, I would like to do a summary of everything right at the end.'

He also asks for disagreement explicitly rather than assuming he will get it: 'I want you to have some pushback if you don't agree with something, don't just go with whatever I'm saying.' The stated purpose behind all of it is deliberate practice — he treats platonic friendships as rehearsal space for a future marriage, on the reasoning that in a romantic relationship 'not speaking for a day isn't an option'.
findings.counter_evidence: This is not a wariness of outside help in general — he asked for and readily accepted a large amount of framework and analysis, and the boundary is only at having words put in his mouth. More awkwardly for the claim, he took on a friend's diagnostic label for his own behaviour without visible scrutiny and acted on it within days by ending a friendship, which is a considerably weaker standard of evidence than he applied to anything else in this thread. The stated motive of practising for a future relationship is self-description, the weakest evidence available; the behavioural corroboration is the repeated refusal of drafts, not the statement itself.

findings.title: Will not apologise for something he cannot name
findings.body:
Mid-conflict, unable to identify what he had done, he refused to apologise anyway: 'I would 100% apologize for what I did here, but (again) I'm not really sure what it is so it would be an empty apology.' The principle held at cost — the message it appeared in was read by Shereen as him centring his own confusion, and the exchange deteriorated from there.

The inverse holds too. Six weeks later, when he could name the fault precisely, the apology was immediate and carried no hedging or counter-claim: 'You're right to question me, you didn't do anything wrong in this case. This one's all me,' followed by a full account of what he had done and when he should have acted differently.
findings.counter_evidence: It is not an absolute refusal — in the same exchange he offered a conditional apology, 'I wasn't making a joke, and I'm sorry if it came across that way', so the line falls at apologising for an unspecified fault rather than at apologising under uncertainty. Nothing here settles whether the principle is integrity about not performing contrition, or a way of deferring the discomfort of conceding fault he does not yet understand; both readings fit the evidence.

open_questions: Did the assumption-alignment conversation actually take place after Shereen's two-week trip, and what surfaced in it?
What did the two-week period of separate prayer and evaluation conclude?

Is 'panicked detachment' an accurate description of his pattern, or a borrowed label from one friend's off-the-cuff read? He acted on it decisively without testing it, and the trigger condition did not hold in the case that prompted it.
He said his previous attempts at shared decision-making 'backfired in my face time after time' — what those cases were, and whether they were genuinely comparable, is never examined.
He was advised to look at whether a trauma-informed therapist would help; no response either way.
